paras: The lynching of Robert Bennett was the killing of a young Black preacher on July 4, 1895, after a mob took him from the pulpit of a church at Hope Henry, five miles west of Lake City, Florida. He was accused of an assault on a white girl or woman, an accusation the reports give in differing forms. In August several white men were charged with the lynching and discharged at a preliminary trial, and the case drew an indignation meeting at Lake City and comment in the Black press.

According to a wire from Lake City, Bennett was lynched for an attempted assault on the little daughter of W. B. Pagett, spelled Padgett in other versions. A press dispatch quoted in the Afro-American instead said his offense was an assault upon a white woman in "Sewanee County," from where the lynchers were said to have come.

On July 4, a party took Bennett from the pulpit of a colored church at Hope Henry, carried him a short distance off and killed him. His body was found by the roadside, and "the usual warning" was left attached to it. Accounts of how he died differ: one news summary said he was hanged, while Albion W. Tourgee's list of July mob killings recorded him as shot.

Citizens of Lake City held an indignation meeting over the lynching, which a news summary described as well attended by both races. Governor Mitchell offered a $500 reward for the arrest and conviction of the lynchers, though the Lake City correspondent wrote that it was not thought the state would ever have to pay it.

On August 20 a preliminary trial was held at Lake City for John Walker, J. M. Rhodan, W. B. Padgett, Thomas Phillips and, in one version, L. D. Padgett, all charged with the lynching. Most versions called the accused white men, though the Birmingham Age-Herald's text listed Rhodan as "colored" and the weekly summaries gave him as "J. M. Rodan, M. D." There was little evidence against the accused, and they were discharged.

About fifty heavily armed white men, friends of the accused, came to town for the hearing "to see that the negroes did not attempt to harm them." A rumor that a carload of armed Black men was coming from Jacksonville to lynch the prisoners led the mayor to close all the saloons. Many Black residents were in town, but the correspondent reported that they made no demonstration and the expected trouble did not occur.

The white press reported the case mainly through the trial wire, a special to the Jacksonville Times-Union that ran on August 21 in the Birmingham Age-Herald as "THE LYNCHING OF THAT PREACHER" and in the Savannah Morning News as "ALLEGED LYNCHERS TRIED." These versions called Bennett "the negro preacher," stated the accusation against him as the reason for the lynching, and doubted the reward would be paid. The Jersey City News headed a shortened version "WHO LYNCHED THE PREACHER?", and a one-sentence brief on the discharge ran in weekly news summaries, among them the News Boy of Benton, Missouri, and the Macon Beacon of Mississippi, from August 29 to September 5.

A letter to The Sun of New York on August 31, "VICTIMS OF MOB LAW," reprinted Tourgee's July list, which included "The Rev. Robert Bennett" as shot and "said to have attempted outrage on white woman." The same day the Afro-American published "THE LYNCHING BUSINESS," an essay from Tourgee's paper that used the dispatch on Bennett as its example of how vague reports excused lynching. The essay mocked the dispatch's account of the alleged crime ("What woman? Oh, a woman.") and described Bennett as a preacher "murdered and mutilated" on a mere report.

The accusation differs between the Lake City wire, which names the little daughter of W. B. Padgett, and the dispatch in the Afro-American, which speaks of an unnamed white woman in Sewanee County. The wire also lists W. B. Padgett among the men charged with the lynching, and the manner of death is given as hanging in one report and as shooting in another.

reader.title: Lynching of Robert Bennett
bases: A mob or 'party' seized Robert Bennett, a Black preacher, from his pulpit and killed him on an accusation of assault (A1, A8), and white men were later charged with lynching him (A2, A3).

Bennett was taken from his pulpit by a mob and killed (A1, A8, A12) with no legal authority, four or five men were charged with the lynching (A2, A3), and the killing was attributed to an alleged assault on a white girl or woman (A3, A8).

A Lake City wire on the trial (A2, A3), a separate press dispatch quoted in the Black press (A8), a news-summary item on an indignation meeting (A1) and Tourgee's list (A12) agree that Bennett, a Black preacher, was lynched near Lake City on July 4.

framing.detail: Southern dailies ran the Lake City wire under 'THE LYNCHING OF THAT PREACHER' and 'ALLEGED LYNCHERS TRIED', calling Bennett 'the negro preacher', stating the accusation flatly and adding that the reward would likely never be paid.
The Jersey City News headed its version 'WHO LYNCHED THE PREACHER?'; weeklies ran a one-sentence trial brief in news summaries.
A letter to The Sun, 'VICTIMS OF MOB LAW', listed Bennett among Tourgee's July victims as evidence of growing lawlessness.
The Afro-American's 'THE LYNCHING BUSINESS' used the Bennett dispatch as its example of how vague reports excuse lynching: 'What woman? Oh, a woman.'

conflicts.note: The Lake City wire of the trial is local and later; the Black-press dispatch is an earlier report of the lynching itself. Neither gives evidence for the charge.

record_check.record: The brains were shot out, the throat cut and both ears cut off; a warning was left on the body.
record_check.dossier: Only the warning left on the body is reported (A8); no report describes the brains shot out, throat cut or ears cut off. Method is given as hanged (A1) or shot (A12).
A mob or party; John Walker, J. M. Rhodan, L. D. and W. B. Padgett and Thomas Phillips were charged and discharged at a preliminary trial on Aug. 20.

record_check.dossier: That is the Lake City wire's version (spelled Pagett or Padgett); a Black-press dispatch says an assault on a white woman in Sewanee County.
No county is named for the lynching; the papers give Lake City and Hope Henry, five miles west.
Also covered in the Black press (Afro-American, Aug. 31) and in at least 12 white papers.
Supported: seized from the pulpit, killed, warning left on the body.
